name: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090
disclaimer: Illustrative geometry drawn to the same 4 mm/unit scale as other chips in this set. Die drawn at ~608 mm² (confirmed); exact die outline, SM grid layout, GDDR6X chip placement and ROP/video-engine positions are symbolic, not a real floorplan.

components.name: Package substrate
components.desc: Standard organic flip-chip substrate, the same kind of package a gaming GPU has used for two decades. No CoWoS, no interposer, no HBM to route — GDDR6X chips wire-bond straight onto the board next to the die, which is why a 4090 costs a fraction of a data-center HBM part per GB.

components.name: AD102 die
components.desc: A single monolithic die on TSMC's custom **4N** process — no multi-die packaging, no die-to-die link. AD102 is NVIDIA's largest Ada die, built for a graphics card first: it carries a full graphics pipeline (RT cores, ROPs, texture units, display engine) alongside the Tensor Core path that AI workloads use. The GeForce RTX 4090 ships a cut-down AD102: **128 of 144 SMs enabled** and **72 of 96 MB of L2 enabled** — the fully-enabled die is reserved for the RTX 6000 Ada / L40 workstation and data-center parts.

specs.label: SMs enabled
specs.value: 128 of 144 on the full AD102 die (18 disabled)

components.name: L2 cache
components.desc: 72 MB enabled out of 96 MB on the full AD102 die — a 12x jump over the RTX 3090's 6 MB. Shared by every SM. On gaming workloads it buffers G-buffer and BVH traffic between ROPs/RT cores and GDDR6X; on AI workloads it holds the weight/activation tiles TMA-free load/store instructions feed to the Tensor Cores, cutting how often a matmul has to go back to GDDR6X.

specs.label: L2 cache (enabled)
specs.value: 72 MB (96 MB on the full AD102 die)

components.name: GDDR6X memory controllers
components.desc: 384-bit aggregate GDDR6X PHY (12 × 32-bit channels around the die perimeter). GDDR6X's PAM4 signaling pushes more bits per pin than classic GDDR6, letting a consumer card reach HBM-class bandwidth-per-dollar without TSVs or an interposer — the trade-off is lower total bandwidth than an HBM-equipped data-center GPU.

components.name: ROPs (render output units)
components.desc: 176 render output units: blend shaded pixels, resolve MSAA and write the final frame to the framebuffer. This is the tail end of the **graphics pipeline** — the part a gamer's frame-rate counter actually measures. It has nothing to do with the Tensor Core matmul path an AI workload uses, which is exactly why a gamer and an AI developer can stare at the same die and describe two completely different GPUs: one cares about triangles-to-pixels throughput through RT cores/ROPs, the other cares about FLOPs-per-byte through Tensor Cores and GDDR6X bandwidth.

components.name: Display engine
components.desc: Drives up to 4 independent displays over DisplayPort 1.4a / HDMI 2.1, with hardware scanout, HDR tone-mapping and the DLSS 3 Frame Generation output path. Entirely separate hardware from the Tensor Core/matmul datapath — a data-center Hopper/Blackwell GPU has no equivalent block at all.

components.name: Video encode/decode engines
components.desc: Dual 8th-generation NVENC encoders with AV1 support (roughly 2x the encode throughput of a single-NVENC Ampere card) plus a 5th-generation NVDEC decoder. Used for streaming/export in Studio workloads and for RTX Video Super Resolution — a third workload sharing the die that neither the gaming nor the AI framing usually accounts for.

components.name: PCIe 4.0 x16
components.desc: GeForce Ada has **no NVLink** — NVIDIA reserves die-to-die/GPU-to-GPU links for data-center and workstation parts (B200, H200, RTX 6000 Ada). A 4090 talks to the host and to any second card purely over PCIe 4.0 x16 (64 GB/s). Multi-GPU training/inference on 4090s has to shard over PCIe instead of a fast fabric, which is the main reason they scale worse than NVLink-equipped parts past 2 GPUs.

components.name: SMs (128 enabled)
components.desc: 128 Streaming Multiprocessors, grouped into 12 GPCs (Graphics Processing Clusters) — AD102 has 144 SMs total across 12 GPCs; the 4090 disables 16 of them for yield/segmentation. Each SM carries both the graphics pipeline hardware (1 RT core, 4 texture units) and the AI-relevant hardware (4 Tensor Cores, 128 CUDA cores). Click **Open SM** to look inside.

components.name: GDDR6X chips (left bank)
components.desc: Discrete GDDR6X packages surface-mounted on the substrate around the die — no TSV stack, no HBM base die, no interposer. 24 GB total across 12 chips (2 GB each, 32-bit wide), split across left and right banks here.

specs.label: Chip count / arrangement
specs.value: Drawn as 12 packages (6 left, 6 right); real board layout varies by AIB partner

components.name: GDDR6X chips (right bank)
components.desc: Second bank of GDDR6X packages, mirroring the left bank.

components.name: L1 / Shared memory
components.desc: Unified, configurable L1 data cache / shared memory per SM, carried over from Ampere's design. Ada's SM has no Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA) like Hopper/Blackwell — ordinary load/store and cp.async instructions move tiles here from L2 for both the graphics pipeline (vertex/pixel data) and the Tensor Core path (matmul operands).

components.name: Tensor Core (4th gen)
components.desc: 4 per SM (512 total). 4th-generation Tensor Cores add **FP8** support over Ampere's 3rd-gen (FP16/BF16/TF32/INT8) and roughly double raw per-core throughput — this is almost the entire reason an AI developer and a gamer see such different GPUs in the same part: an AI inference job spends nearly all its time issuing matmuls here, while a game barely touches these cores except through DLSS. No FP4 support on Ada — that arrives with Blackwell.

components.name: RT Core (3rd gen)
components.desc: 1 per SM (128 total). Walks the BVH and tests ray/triangle + ray/box intersections in fixed-function hardware. 3rd-gen adds Opacity Micromaps and Displacement Micro-Meshes for faster alpha-test and geometry-heavy ray tracing. This is the heart of the **graphics-pipeline view** of this chip — it never executes a single matmul, and an AI-only workload leaves it completely idle.

components.name: Texture units
components.desc: 4 per SM (512 total). Fetch and filter texture/surface data for the graphics pipeline — sampling, mip-mapping, anisotropic filtering. Also reused by some AI codepaths for fast interpolated lookups, but their primary job is shading rasterized pixels.

components.name: Register file
components.desc: Per-thread registers, one slice per SM sub-partition (4 partitions per SM). Tensor Core MMA accumulators live here directly — unlike Blackwell's dedicated Tensor Memory, Ada has no separate accumulator store.

components.name: Warp scheduler + CUDA cores
components.desc: 4 partitions per SM, each issuing one warp (32 threads) per cycle to its 32 scalar CUDA cores (FP32/INT32). Runs the epilogue after a Tensor Core MMA — bias add, activation, requantize to FP8 — and runs ordinary shader math for the graphics pipeline.

steps.text: 1. Weights/activations (AI) or vertex/texture data (graphics) sit in GDDR6X — 24 GB at 1,008 GB/s over a 384-bit bus.
2. The GDDR6X memory controller reads the die's request. GDDR6X's PAM4 signaling gets HBM-adjacent bandwidth from ordinary package pins — no interposer needed.
3. Data lands in the shared 72 MB L2 cache (96 MB total on the full AD102 die, cut down for the 4090).
4. Ordinary load/store instructions copy the matmul tile from L2 into the SM's L1/shared memory — Ada has no TMA, unlike Hopper/Blackwell.
5. The 4th-gen Tensor Cores multiply the tile, now with FP8 support alongside FP16/BF16/TF32/INT8 — this is almost 100% of what an AI inference job spends its time on.
6. Partial sums accumulate directly in the register file — Ada has no dedicated Tensor Memory, so results never leave registers mid-accumulation. Steps 4-6 repeat along K.
7. Epilogue: CUDA cores add bias, apply activation, and quantize the result back to FP8 or FP16.
8. Results write back through L2 to GDDR6X. With no NVLink on GeForce Ada, a second GPU can only be reached over PCIe 4.0 x16 (64 GB/s) — far slower than a data-center part's NVLink fabric.

9. Graphics aside: a ray-tracing workload instead sends BVH traversal to the RT core in fixed-function hardware — it never touches the Tensor Cores at all, which is why a gamer's mental model of this chip looks nothing like an AI developer's.

10. The shaded, ray-traced pixels leave the SM through the ROPs and are scanned out by the display engine — the finish line a gamer's FPS counter measures, and a block an AI-only data-center GPU doesn't even have.
